title: The Department of Things That Fit Into Other Things
subtitle: Puzzles, mechanisms, creative toys and retro desktop diversions

opening.title: The Cabinet Refuses the Binder
paragraphs: I bought the cabinet because its label said STORAGE SOLUTION. I considered this a binding professional promise. The cabinet arrived flat, which was the first sign that it expected me to participate in the solution. Tank carried the pieces inside and laid them next to the table. Shawna found the instructions. I found the decorative nameplate I had ordered separately and placed it where the finished cabinet would eventually have a chest.

'You bought a nameplate before checking the measurements,' Mercedes said. 'A institution needs an identity,' I replied. 'It also needs to fit through the doorway.' Rosa brought tea, examined the wall and quietly moved a vase beyond the area in which my confidence was most likely to cause damage. Tank held two boards together. The pieces looked deceptively simple. There were only a few shapes, a small bag of fittings, and an unlimited number of ways for me to explain that the problem was somebody else's.

The binder was supposed to go in the top compartment. It did not. I turned it sideways. The cabinet declined. I removed a page, which reduced the thickness by an amount Tank described as emotionally significant. Shawna asked why I had started assembling a storage system around an object without measuring the object. I told her the binder represented a living vision. She handed me a tape measure. 'Then let's see how long it lives.'

This was the moment the Department of Things That Fit Into Other Things discovered its subject. A puzzle can use a few familiar actions and still ask a wonderfully difficult question. A quiet board can offer deep reasoning. A richly rendered cabinet can conceal a control that needs a held drag. An attractive cartoon can contain a severe logic problem, while a serious-looking mechanism can become perfectly readable once somebody shows you what moves. Appearance and physical demand had been filing reports in the same folder. Shawna separated them.

I proposed three labels: BRILLIANT, EXTREMELY BRILLIANT, and AWAITING MY ARRIVAL. Mercedes crossed them out. Rosa wrote two actual questions on an index card: Do I want to know what happens? Does doing it feel good? Tank added a third: Is Aiden standing on the instructions? I stepped aside. Under my shoe, a diagram showed the shelf fitted the other way around. The cabinet had not been refusing the binder. It had been refusing my interpretation of a rectangle.

We agreed that the book could contain difficult reasoning without pretending every difficulty was the same. A game could wait patiently while a person considered a complicated relationship. Another could demand a quick movement despite its thoughtful story. A puzzle about changing rules might be exciting; a menu full of tiny icons might merely be tedious. The job was to say which activity was actually on offer, identify the catch, and leave the decision with the person who would play.

I tried to turn this agreement into a certification scheme. Shawna said a useful description would do. I tried to add a compulsory introductory lecture. Rosa said the tea would get cold. Mercedes selected a page directly, bypassing my entire route system, and the floor remained under us. Tank fitted the shelf correctly. The binder still protruded a little, but the cabinet now served a purpose. I attached the nameplate on the inside, where its authority would interfere with fewer people.

interludes.title: The Undo Budget
paragraphs: I established an Undo Budget after noticing how often a puzzle could become interesting precisely when an earlier idea turned out to be wrong. The proposal included a request form, a committee and a modest administrative charge payable in public acknowledgment of my foresight. Tank asked whether we could undo the proposal. I said that would require the form. Shawna tore the form in half. Apparently the department had discovered a direct-action interface.

Rosa put two of the cabinet's spare fittings on the table. She moved one, considered the result, then put it back. 'That's all,' she said. 'Sometimes trying an idea is how you find out what the problem is.' Mercedes added that a mistake should not automatically become a performance review. I had been preparing a report on the fitting's lack of ambition, so this intervention saved everyone several pages.

Undo and restart still needed to be checked in the actual game. We could not award them by wishing, and we could not assume that a feature in one installment existed in another. But when a useful reversal was present, it changed the feeling of experimentation. A move could be a question. An unsuccessful arrangement could leave behind a better understanding. Nobody had to preserve the first idea simply because I had stamped it.

I attempted to undo my purchase of the oversized binder. Tank said that feature belonged to the shop's returns policy, not the puzzle. We found a practical alternative: divide the contents into smaller volumes and keep the route card visible. It was not a spectacular solution, which made it unusually easy to explain. I claimed the improvement as a triumph of iterative leadership. Mercedes asked whether she could undo that sentence. We let her.

interludes.title: A Quiet Board Can Contain a Loud Problem
paragraphs: At the next meeting I displayed two pictures. One was a cheerful creature. The other was an ornate machine surrounded by impressive shadows. I asked the committee which was easier. Shawna asked, 'Easier to move, easier to understand, easier to read, or easier to stop thinking about?' This was an unreasonable number of useful questions for a presentation that had originally contained only two slides.

Tank said the creature could require a difficult sequence of moves. Mercedes said the machine might be lovely to inspect even if she needed a clue. Rosa said neither picture told us whether somebody had to hold a button while doing something else. I looked at my labels, which read FRIENDLY and IMPORTANT. They did not survive the discussion.

We replaced the labels with descriptions of actions. Moving one square. Turning an object. Holding and dragging a piece. Reading a clue. Remembering which room contained a symbol. Waiting for a safe moment to pass a guard. These were not interchangeable demands, and none of them could be inferred reliably from the amount of gold trim on the screen. The book's quieter page design suddenly seemed more useful than my attempted hierarchy of seriousness.

I wanted to preserve one grand distinction: a grown-up evening could include simple play without needing to apologize for it. Mercedes agreed, provided we also acknowledged the opposite. A person who wanted complicated characters should not be handed a coloring toy merely because its controls were small. Taste was part of the decision. We returned both pictures to the table with better descriptions. The creature kept its dignity. The machine lost its automatic promotion. I lost a slide deck, which everyone described as an improvement.

interludes.title: The Museum of Working Things
paragraphs: We opened the retro cabinet with appropriate ceremony. Tank held the door so it would not strike the table. I announced that every artifact within had survived an era of inferior management and therefore deserved respect. Shawna asked which one currently worked on the available equipment. The ceremony paused while the museum encountered the difference between historical interest and an actual evening's entertainment.

A mouse from an old console suggested a small creative studio. A city simulator suggested systems, budgets and a skyline. A contraption builder suggested a ball reaching an objective by the most entertaining possible route. These were distinct invitations. Mercedes refused to let the single word retro make them interchangeable. Rosa also refused to let nostalgia turn setup trouble into a social obligation. A lovely memory could stay lovely without everyone spending the evening chasing an unavailable driver.

We wrote down what was known from a manual or an exact-edition source and what still needed checking. A source gap stayed a source gap. A scan we could locate but not read did not become a control audit because I looked solemn beside it. I offered to issue a provisional seal. Shawna said the plain sentence about the gap was already doing more useful work than the seal would.

Tank found the red stapler in the cabinet and asked whether I intended to classify it as a historical pointing device. I said its original firmware was still intact. He stapled two loose sheets, demonstrating compatibility with paper. That was the strongest hands-on evidence produced during the ceremony. We left the cabinet open, placed the useful notes beside it, and agreed that an old favorite should earn its place through present enjoyment, with history allowed to make the invitation warmer.

ending.title: The Last Compartment
paragraphs: By the end of the department's review, the cabinet contained fewer things than I had intended and more things we could actually find. The gold stamp had a small space of its own. The red stapler sat where a hand could reach it. The binder had become several manageable volumes. Tank opened the door and closed it again without holding the entire structure steady, which I described as a major infrastructure milestone. He described it as a cabinet.

We did not finish every puzzle in order to justify their existence. Some pages made somebody curious immediately. Others revealed a catch that settled the choice just as usefully. A drag could be unwelcome. A dense logic board could be exactly the right invitation. A beautifully told mystery could still include timing that ruled it out for a particular evening. The point of the collection was to make those differences visible before my enthusiasm tried to run over them with a ceremonial trolley.

Mercedes chose a page because she liked the premise, then checked the burden before considering the first action. Rosa set the tea where nobody had to reach across the book. Shawna left a blank line beside an unresolved control question. Tank put the spare fittings in a small bag and wrote CABINET on it. I admired the economy of that label while privately considering whether Cabinet Affairs would sound more established.

There was one compartment left. I proposed reserving it for future expansion. Mercedes suggested leaving it empty until something worth keeping appeared. This felt dangerously unambitious until I noticed how calm the shelf looked without a speculative monument to my plans. An empty place was not a failure to choose. It was room for the next thing that actually appealed.

I put away the final form. Nobody had signed it, and nothing important had gone wrong. The guest could pick a puzzle, return to a story, try a creative toy, or close the book. The cabinet did not award points for finishing its contents. Neither, after a brief and unsuccessful attempt to add a scoring drawer, did I. Tank shut the door. For once the department's most convincing achievement was that everything useful remained easy to reach.

games.title: Baba Is You
games.case_title: The Law Has Been Pushed One Square to the Left
scene: I wrote AIDEN IS IN CHARGE on a card and placed it at the head of the table. Shawna removed IN CHARGE and replaced it with FURNITURE. Tank immediately asked whether I was available to support the snack bowl. I objected that words could not simply alter the governing order. Then we opened Baba Is You, which made that argument difficult to sustain.

The little blocks did more than describe the world. Moving them changed what the world allowed. Rosa experimented with a sentence instead of defending the first arrangement. Mercedes asked whether my title was useful if it prevented us from reaching the interesting part. I considered this a suspiciously specific philosophical attack. Then a rule changed, the puzzle opened in a new direction and I forgot to be offended. The card at the head of the table now read AIDEN IS THINKING. For once, nobody challenged its accuracy.
games.pleasure: Baba Is You turns the rules of a puzzle into objects you can move. A short arrangement of words can transform what a wall, flag or character does. The appeal is the surprise of realizing that the rule you assumed was fixed is actually the thing to manipulate.
games.burden: The small number of movement actions should not be confused with easy reasoning. The developer describes a large collection of increasingly inventive rule interactions. Reading the words, predicting consequences and revising a plan can become demanding. Check the exact movement, undo and restart controls rather than assuming they are comfortable because the board is compact.
games.first: Try an introductory level and deliberately move one rule word. Observe what changes before attempting a long solution or consulting an entire set of hints.
games.ruling: The legislature authorizes rewriting the wall, but nobody is required to solve grammar's revenge before enjoying a biscuit.

games.title: Patrick's Parabox
games.case_title: The Storage Box Contains the Storage Department
scene: I bought a box to hold the smaller boxes. This was a sensible beginning. Then I discovered a box that contained itself, and my inventory system suffered a spiritual injury. Tank asked whether we could put the binder inside it and recover the table. I said the implications required study. He said the table required space.

Shawna pushed one box and demonstrated that the strange rule could be understood through an ordinary action. Rosa followed the relationship between the outside and the inside. Mercedes suggested that I stop trying to name every layer before moving anything. I did, and the puzzle became less like an insult from mathematics and more like a toy with an unfamiliar but learnable grammar. The storage department remained confused about its office address. That was acceptable. We had reached a point where confusion was producing curiosity instead of another requisition form.
games.pleasure: Patrick's Parabox explores boxes that contain other boxes, including recursive arrangements. The repeated act of pushing gains new meaning as the space folds into itself. Its interest is in discovering how a small set of relationships can support surprisingly rich puzzles.
games.burden: The current Steam listing declares play without timed input and keyboard-only support. Spatial nesting can still require holding several relationships in mind even when the controls are limited. Verify key repeat, undo and any zoom behavior in the actual version. There is little conventional character story to carry the experience if the recursive logic itself does not appeal.
games.first: Play the earliest introduction to entering and leaving a box. Explain one relationship aloud if useful, then try a move that tests that explanation.
games.ruling: The Department of Storage may now fit inside its own cabinet, but its annual report must remain shorter than the cabinet.
games.source_note: Exact Steam developer description supports premise. Current developer declarations include Playable without Timed Input and Keyboard Only Option. Physical comfort, held inputs and reasoning load still need their stated checks; this is not a hands-on completion test.

games.title: Stephen's Sausage Roll
games.case_title: The Catering Subcommittee Has Become a Logic Problem
scene: I assumed the sausage would be the easiest item on the agenda. This was before the fork, the narrow space and my rapidly declining confidence became involved. Tank watched me consider the arrangement. 'You could admit you need to think.' 'I am allowing the ingredients to reveal their strategy.'

Rosa asked whether the sausage had consented to becoming a strategic actor. Shawna suggested making one move and seeing what it taught us. Mercedes declined my proposal to call the situation a catering emergency. There was no emergency. There was a small, exact problem that did not care how confidently I described it. I found that annoying and then, unexpectedly, satisfying. A better idea arrived only after I stopped trying to make my first idea look correct. Tank said this was the most educational lunch we had never eaten. I asked him not to put that on the menu.
games.pleasure: Stephen's Sausage Roll is a compact three-dimensional puzzle game built around unusually exact spatial problems. Its appeal is the satisfaction of understanding a small arrangement deeply enough to make it work. It belongs on the reasoning shelf for someone who enjoys a stubborn little mechanism more than an expansive story.
games.burden: The inspected primary storefront supplies very little detailed control information, so this card does not certify timing, holds or the full interaction set. The title's cheerful food premise should not imply easy puzzles. Treat both input comfort and the amount of planning as questions for an early trial, with no expectation of quick completion.
games.first: Inspect the first small puzzle and test a single movement. If the rules interest you, try one hypothesis; if they merely irritate, leave the plate unfinished.
games.ruling: The sausage is excused from being dinner and appointed a temporary consultant on the limits of executive confidence.
games.source_note: Exact-game Steam description is very brief ('A simple 3d puzzle game'); source supports identity and basic genre, not detailed control or difficulty certification. Scene is original fiction. Specific input and full-game timing remain to be checked.

games.title: Snakebird
games.case_title: The Bird Has Exceeded the Approved Length for Birds
scene: I requested a bird of standard dimensions. The bird ate fruit and became longer, which I considered an unauthorized amendment to the seating plan. Tank suggested reserving two chairs. Then it grew again. My hospitality model was losing ground to produce.

Shawna asked what the extra length made possible. I had been so busy declaring it inconvenient that I had not considered usefulness. Rosa watched the shape cross a gap in a way a shorter creature could not. Mercedes said a constraint sometimes becomes a tool if you stop insisting it should be something else. I wrote that down, then discovered I had used the entire width of the page. Tank offered a longer sheet and waited for the irony to reach me. Eventually it did. We returned to the puzzle with a better question: not how to make the bird ordinary, but how to use the bird we had.
games.pleasure: Snakebird makes the length and shape of its fruit-eating creatures central to spatial puzzles. What looks like a small comic animal becomes a tool for crossing, supporting and arranging a route. The attraction is the way a simple change in body length changes the whole problem.
games.burden: The developer explicitly calls the game deceptively challenging. A friendly drawing and a small board should not be sold as easy reasoning. Check directional input, switching between creatures and recovery from mistakes. The card does not establish universal no-timing behavior from genre alone; its strongest case is for a player who enjoys concentrated spatial experimentation.
games.first: Try the earliest fruit-and-exit arrangement. Notice what the new length permits before attempting to plan several moves ahead.
games.ruling: The bird may exceed the furniture specification; the reader may decline the puzzle without submitting a shorter bird.

games.title: Snakebird Primer
games.case_title: The Orientation Bird Has Brought a Smaller Problem
scene: After our first encounter with an extremely long bird, I commissioned an orientation program. It contained a twenty-page introduction to the concept of fruit. Shawna removed nineteen pages. Tank ate the visual aid on the remaining one. We were forced to begin with the actual game.

The new island introduced its ideas with less apparent hostility to our afternoon. Rosa appreciated having room to learn a pattern before the pattern acquired relatives. Mercedes said a gentler introduction did not make the activity lesser; it made the invitation clearer. I agreed, then tried to call myself the architect of this educational philosophy. Shawna pointed to the developer's name. I withdrew the claim and concentrated on the creature in front of us. One small success led naturally to another question. This was a much better orientation than my speech about the historic significance of the banana.
games.pleasure: Snakebird Primer is a separate set of puzzles designed as a more approachable introduction to Snakebird's spatial ideas. The developer explicitly contrasts its easier island with the original game's serious challenges. It can be a useful place to discover whether moving and shaping these creatures is pleasurable before choosing the harder title.
games.burden: Easier is a comparison, not a personal guarantee. Directional movement, visual planning and keeping track of a changing shape still matter. Check undo, restart and control repetition in the exact release. The appeal remains puzzle logic rather than rich character dialogue, and a player need not graduate to the original game to justify enjoying this one.
games.first: Complete or explore one introductory arrangement, focusing on how fruit changes the creature. Let curiosity about the next idea decide whether to continue.
games.ruling: The orientation certificate is optional, the banana is gone and nobody has been enrolled in mandatory advanced bird studies.

games.title: A Good Snowman Is Hard To Build
games.case_title: The Snowman Has Asked Me to Stop Calling Him a Deliverable
scene: I set a target of three snowmen before lunch. Rosa asked why. 'A department requires outputs.' She looked at the small monster on the screen, then at me. 'Maybe the monster wants to make one nice snowman.' Tank supported this position, partly because lunch was already approaching without any help from my target.

Shawna studied how the snowballs occupied the space. Mercedes wondered what would happen if I stopped measuring the afternoon by completed figures. I tried making one deliberate move. The little arrangement became interesting in itself: size, position and the order in which things could happen. My production chart began to look ridiculous beside it. I turned the chart over and drew a face on the back. Tank said it was my most useful contribution so far. I gave the face a senior title anyway, because reform is a gradual process.
games.pleasure: A Good Snowman Is Hard To Build makes a small, affectionate premise into a spatial puzzle: a monster creating snowmen. The compact scenes invite attention to a few objects and how their positions relate. It can offer a satisfying repeated activity without needing a sprawling world or a dense inventory story.
games.burden: The current developer listing declares play without timed input and keyboard-only support. Check movement, undo and snowball manipulation on the chosen device; those declarations do not establish that every action avoids holding. The puzzles still require planning and trial, so the gentle presentation should not become a promise of effortless solutions. Narrative is limited to the charm of the activity.
games.first: Try making one snowman and notice where your first plan changes. Learn the recovery control before treating a mistaken move as a reason to restart everything.
games.ruling: The snowman is recognized as a pleasant use of an afternoon and exempted from quarterly productivity reporting.

games.title: Cosmic Express
games.case_title: The Railway Can Carry One Passenger and All of My Mistakes
scene: I promised the aliens a world-class transit system. Then I discovered the passenger car could carry only one of them at a time. Tank asked whether my promise had included capacity planning. I said the service emphasized intimacy. Shawna began drawing a route that actually reached the houses.

Every turn in the track mattered. Rosa considered the passengers as destinations rather than decorative obstacles. Mercedes asked me to stop calling a loop around nowhere a scenic service. I erased the loop. Another route almost worked, which was somehow more interesting than my first confident answer. We watched the small consequences accumulate until the problem became clear. The station did not need a grand announcement. It needed a track that delivered somebody home. I canceled the ribbon ceremony and spent the saved time looking at the final corner. This improved transport more than any of my slogans.
games.pleasure: Cosmic Express asks you to lay railway routes through small space stations and deliver their residents. The one-passenger constraint makes the order of visits important. Its appeal is the clean relationship between a visible route and the consequences that follow from it.
games.burden: The developer describes the puzzles as difficult and separately declares play without timed input, with keyboard-only and mouse-only options. Drawing tracks may still involve sustained pointer actions, so test the intended input method. Cute passengers do not reduce the planning burden: a compact station can hold a demanding puzzle. The declared input options do not certify hold-free interaction.
games.first: Draw a route in an early station and watch one passenger's trip. Test editing or resetting the route before trying to optimize a complicated arrangement.
games.ruling: The railway is authorized to be small, provided it goes somewhere more useful than the minister's opening speech.
games.source_note: Exact Steam developer description supports premise. Current developer declarations include Playable without Timed Input and Keyboard Only Option plus Mouse Only Option. Physical comfort, held inputs and reasoning load still need their stated checks; this is not a hands-on completion test.

games.title: A Monster's Expedition
games.case_title: The Museum Has Mistaken My Stapler for a Ceremonial Animal
scene: I have always believed ordinary office equipment deserves more respect. Then the monsters began interpreting human objects, and I discovered that respect can take a very strange shape when nobody knows what anything was for. Tank said the red stapler did look like a small creature with a bad attitude.

Rosa read the exhibit with delight. Shawna examined the little island and the tree that might become a path. Mercedes asked whether our own explanations of unfamiliar things were always more reliable. I began to answer confidently, then remembered several recent incidents involving birds, boxes and an allegedly criminal shrub. We tried moving the tree instead. It produced a concrete result, unlike my lecture. The next island held another object and another chance to be amused by certainty. I quietly changed my proposed museum plaque from 'Authoritative History' to 'A Person Had a Guess.'
games.pleasure: A Monster's Expedition combines tree-pushing spatial puzzles with comic museum observations about humanity. Small islands form a larger exploratory structure, so solving a route can lead to both a new place and a new joke. It offers a particular mix of thoughtful manipulation and dry amusement.
games.burden: The developer describes simple mechanics with substantial depth. That depth can mean difficult planning even when the action vocabulary is small. Check movement, undo, reset and the readability of the islands and exhibits. Its open structure should not be treated as proof that every puzzle is optional or that every route remains easy.
games.first: Solve or experiment with one early crossing, then read the nearby exhibit. Judge whether the combination of puzzle and joke makes you want another island.
games.ruling: The stapler may remain a ceremonial animal until someone produces evidence that its bite served a different social purpose.

games.title: Bonfire Peaks
games.case_title: The Archive Has Been Asked to Consider Letting Something Go
scene: I objected to the premise on professional grounds. An archive exists to keep things. The game appeared interested in leaving them behind. Tank looked at the three binders beneath my chair and said the game might have a point. I said those binders contained important historical context. Shawna opened one. It contained old versions of the same seating chart.

Rosa suggested that choosing what to release could be as meaningful as collecting. Mercedes added that a difficult object did not become valuable merely because I had carried it a long way. This was a troubling conversation to have beside a puzzle about movement and cargo. I tried arranging the next few steps without defending the entire archive. The small physical problem gave the larger idea room to breathe. I did not immediately throw away a binder. I did, however, admit that one of them could become a doorstop without betraying civilization.
games.pleasure: Bonfire Peaks presents a spatial puzzle journey organized around closure and moving onward. Its compact, sculptural environments make objects and their placement visually central. It may appeal when the satisfaction of an exact arrangement is strengthened by a quiet theme about what people carry.
games.burden: The primary description promises rewarding challenges and evolving mechanics, not low difficulty. Manipulating objects in three-dimensional puzzle spaces may require careful orientation and planning. Check the actual movement and object controls before assuming the fixed-looking presentation eliminates physical demands. The emotional theme is suggestive rather than a richly voiced character drama.
games.first: Inspect an early puzzle, learn one object interaction and test how to recover from a mistake. Continue only if the precise arrangement feels absorbing rather than burdensome.
games.ruling: One obsolete binder may be released from service; the minister is permitted to survive the loss without commissioning a memorial.

games.title: Can of Wormholes
games.case_title: The Hint Department Has Built a Smaller Puzzle Instead of a Lecture
scene: I opened the can expecting a manageable administrative issue. Worms were involved, then space behaved strangely, and before long I was considering whether a can could file a complaint against its own contents. Tank said the title had provided adequate warning. I argued that warning and preparation were different budgets.

Shawna noticed the hint system. Instead of simply handing over an answer, it offered a smaller playable idea. Rosa liked that: a nudge that still left discovery in the player's hands. Mercedes asked whether my own explanations could become shorter and more useful in the same way. I said yes, then took four sentences to prove that I had not yet achieved it. We tried the small hint puzzle. Something clicked. The larger problem changed from a wall into a question we could work with. I appointed the tiny puzzle head of training and accepted a probationary role.
games.pleasure: Can of Wormholes develops many interactions from a small collection of puzzle objects. Its distinctive strength for this catalogue is a documented playable hint system: a smaller related stage can suggest the insight needed for the larger one. Experimentation and discovery are the main rewards.
games.burden: The developer explicitly states that no time-critical inputs or simultaneous key presses are required, and documents unlimited undo and restart. Those are unusually useful concrete claims. Keyboard or gamepad play is supported, with a Mac gamepad limitation noted by the developer. Spatial reasoning and learning new interactions can still be demanding; hold behavior should be checked separately.
games.first: Try an introductory stage, use undo once and inspect a playable hint if curiosity stalls. Learn how the support works before a difficult puzzle makes it feel urgent.
games.ruling: The training department is approved because it offers a useful smaller idea instead of requiring attendance at my worm-related keynote.
games.source_note: Developer Steam description explicitly says no time-critical input or simultaneous key presses, unlimited undo/restart and playable hints; gamepad on Mac is not currently supported in that description. This supports the stated narrow timing claims, not universal hold-free operation.

games.title: Braid, Anniversary Edition
games.case_title: I Would Like to Rewind the Part Where I Announced Expertise
scene: The ability to reverse time struck me as the most promising administrative reform in history. I could retract an entire speech without issuing a correction. Tank asked whether I would use it before or after we had heard the speech. I said the implementation details were still being negotiated.

Then the game made time part of a puzzle rather than a service for preserving my reputation. Shawna watched how the rules changed between places. Rosa noticed the memories and regrets woven into the journey. Mercedes pointed out that undoing an action and understanding it were not the same thing. I had been hoping they were. We tried a movement again, this time with a different idea. It was satisfying, but it still required the movement. The rewind did not transform my hands into a committee. I recorded that distinction before my enthusiasm could accidentally turn it into a promise.
games.pleasure: Braid, Anniversary Edition combines platform movement with puzzles built around unusual behavior of time. Its story and images concern memory, desire and regret. The new edition also includes extensive creator commentary, offering another route into the design for someone interested in how a game thinks.
games.burden: Rewinding does not remove jumping, hazards or required movement timing. The developer explicitly describes platforming and changing time mechanics. This is a conditional action-puzzle detour, not a standard no-rush fit. Check movement, jump combinations and rewind holds separately; a forgiving recovery system can reduce failure cost without reducing the action itself.
games.first: Try one introductory movement puzzle and the rewind control. If the physical action is unwelcome, consider the design commentary as an interest to investigate rather than forcing play.
games.ruling: The minister may revise a mistaken move, but the laws of time decline to erase every embarrassing claim of competence.

games.title: World of Goo
games.case_title: The Bridge Is Held Together by Optimism and a Concerning Amount of Goo
scene: I approved the bridge design because it looked ambitious. Tank asked whether ambition could bear weight. I said history was full of structures people had doubted. Shawna suggested this was not a substitute for examining the lower connection. The lower connection chose that moment to prove her point.

The little living pieces made construction feel less like drawing a line and more like persuading a crowd to hold hands in a dangerous shape. Rosa wanted them to arrive somewhere useful. Mercedes wanted me to stop naming unfinished bridges after myself. I tried a shorter structure. It held a little longer. Another adjustment changed the balance. Soon we were watching cause and effect rather than defending a glorious silhouette. The company in the game appeared to have its own questionable priorities. I felt personally attacked by several of them and therefore suspected the satire was functioning correctly.
games.pleasure: World of Goo turns drag-and-drop construction into a physics puzzle with a comic corporate world around it. Structures bend, balance and fail in visible ways, so a small design change can be satisfying to test. Its personality comes from the creatures, signs and increasingly strange purposes of the construction work.
games.burden: The primary description explicitly says drag and drop. Holding and positioning the pointer may therefore be a central barrier. Physics unfolds while structures are running, and hazards vary by level, so do not assume an unlimited-waiting solution from the word puzzle. Check the ordinary building loop before becoming invested in the larger campaign.
games.first: Build the smallest useful connection in an early level and watch it behave. Test selecting, dragging and releasing one piece before attempting an elaborate tower.
games.ruling: The bridge may carry traffic after it carries itself; the commemorative nameplate can wait indefinitely.

scene: The object looked expensive, secretive and difficult to open. Naturally, I assumed it belonged in my office. Tank asked what it did. 'It establishes atmosphere.' Every surface seemed capable of concealing a latch, a clue or another arrangement of parts. Rosa enjoyed the invitation to look closely. Mercedes asked whether I could resist declaring the first discovery a final victory. I said yes and immediately tried to announce a breakthrough. The next layer opened, proving that the breakthrough had merely acquired a hallway. We laughed and kept looking. The pleasure was not in owning the box or displaying it beside my nameplate. It was in finding the small thing that changed what the box could become. I considered that an improvement in my relationship with office equipment.

Connecting many identities and events can also impose a large memory burden, while the ship's fate involves death and disturbing material. The inspected primary description is brief; it does not establish every timing or interaction requirement. Choose it for substantial deduction, not as a low-effort introduction to mysteries.
games.first: Inspect the opening environment and the investigation interface. Check visual comfort and navigation before deciding whether maintaining a larger network of people and clues sounds enjoyable.
games.ruling: Admit the investigator only after checking the ship's controls. My soup certificate will not be accepted as evidence of maritime expertise.

games.title: Opus Magnum
games.case_title: The Machine Works but the Management Has Opinions
scene: I wanted a machine that would place the gold stamp on a page, admire the result, and then quietly perform all the work the stamp implied. Opus Magnum appeared more interested in making transformations actually happen. Tank said this was already an improvement on the department's current business model.

Programmable arms, tracks and repeating operations gave my imaginary workshop a clear question: could this arrangement produce the required result? Shawna built a small logical explanation while I considered a ceremonial name for the machine. Mercedes said a working solution could be enough, even if somebody else's was smaller or faster. That statement threatened the entire Bureau of Comparative Excellence, so I took a moment to process it. Rosa suggested watching the parts move once they were doing the right thing. There was pleasure in that, separate from winning an argument about efficiency. I approved the first working arrangement and resisted adding an arm whose sole job was to point at my name.
games.pleasure: Opus Magnum is an open-ended machine-building puzzle about arranging and programming alchemical equipment. Several solutions can work, with optional interest in making them cheaper, smaller or faster. A story of ambition and intrigue surrounds the workshop, while watching a successful mechanism repeat its work provides a distinctive reward.
games.burden: The editor, component placement and instruction sequencing create substantial interface and reasoning demands. Optimization comparisons can introduce self-imposed pressure even when a solution already works. Machine execution speed is not the same thing as required human reaction speed, but exact editing holds and all control requirements still need checking. The narrative is woven around construction rather than replacing it.
games.first: Follow one introductory construction and make a single operation work. Ignore efficiency comparisons while deciding whether arranging and revising a machine is enjoyable in itself.
games.ruling: Approve a machine because it works and is satisfying to watch. An extra arm dedicated to congratulating its inventor is not a necessary component.

games.title: Sokobond
games.case_title: The Molecule Has Rejected an Unnecessary Management Layer
scene: I looked at a small arrangement of atoms and proposed adding a supervisor. Shawna explained that this was a chemistry puzzle, not a staffing dispute. 'Everything benefits from coordination,' I said. Tank pointed out that the atoms appeared to be doing substantially better without a meeting.

The appeal was a compact problem that could change meaning as the pieces connected. I did not need to turn the room into a laboratory or pretend I remembered every chemical symbol from school. Mercedes appreciated the promise that prior chemistry knowledge was unnecessary; she wanted to discover the rules through the puzzle itself. Rosa asked whether the quiet presentation hid a serious challenge. It could, which seemed like a fair arrangement if the challenge was enjoyable. I removed the supervisor from my diagram. A small system had enough relationships already. Then I tried to charge the department for the successful removal of an unnecessary position and discovered that everyone remembered who had proposed it.
games.pleasure: Sokobond turns molecular connections into compact logic puzzles with a minimalist presentation. The developer explicitly says chemistry knowledge is not required. Its current Steam declarations include keyboard-only play and play without timed input, making this a useful candidate when deliberate problem-solving is welcome but reaction pressure is not.
games.burden: A small control vocabulary can still support difficult spatial reasoning. Confirm comfortable key presses, any repeat behavior and how undo works on the actual device. The developer's no-timed-input declaration is useful evidence, not a hands-on comfort guarantee. This is mainly abstract puzzle pleasure; it will not supply the character-rich narrative that motivates some other choices in the catalog.
games.first: Try one introductory molecular puzzle and learn the result of a single movement. Continue only if revising a spatial idea feels satisfying, without requiring prior chemistry expertise.
games.ruling: Approve bonds that make a good puzzle. Deny my proposal to place an executive atom above the others and call the arrangement leadership.
games.source_note: Exact Steam source supports chemistry-themed puzzles without required chemistry knowledge. Current developer declarations include Keyboard Only Option and Playable without Timed Input. Those declarations are not a hands-on test of sustained keys or individual comfort. Remote Play Together is not treated as native co-op.

games.title: Hexcells
games.case_title: The Hexagon Has Filed Six Equally Valid Complaints
scene: I chose a hexagonal form because it looked more advanced than the department's rectangles. Tank asked whether six sides made the instructions any clearer. I said the additional edges offered room for innovation. Shawna said they mostly offered room for me to write six versions of the same vague sentence.

A quiet field of cells was a more appealing use of the shape. There could be pleasure in finding one justified move, then letting it reveal another. Mercedes said that sounded like a good reason to sit down if the clues were readable. Rosa suggested removing the theatrical briefing so the actual instructions could be seen. I obliged, reluctantly folding my hexagonal agenda into a shape best described as damaged. The puzzle did not need an invented story about national importance. A visible pattern and a small piece of certainty might be enough. My form was reassigned as a coaster, where its unusually generous perimeter finally served a practical purpose.
games.pleasure: Hexcells is presented by its developer as an ambient logic puzzle. Its compact cell-based format offers a different kind of interest from walking through a world: inspect the board, understand its rules and look for a reasoned next step. It is a candidate for someone who likes deliberate abstract deduction.
games.burden: The inspected primary description is unusually brief, so it does not substantiate a full no-timer or hold-free claim. Check the game's instructions, cell readability and the distinction between its input actions before relying on it. A sparse screen does not guarantee an easy deduction. This original Hexcells entry should not inherit features or extra modes from the separate Plus and Infinite games.
games.first: Read the opening board instructions and make one move whose reason is clear. Check whether selecting and distinguishing cells feels comfortable before increasing the puzzle size.
games.ruling: Grant six-sided logic a hearing if its clues invite another look. The department's hexagonal stationery remains a beverage accessory until its wording improves.
games.source_note: The exact-game Steam page describes an ambient logic puzzle; its short primary text does not establish full controls or timing. The separate sequels' features were not imported. Detailed input verification remains outstanding.

games.title: Tametsi
games.case_title: The Tiles Have Demanded Evidence Before Anyone Touches Them
scene: I arrived with a strategy called Probably That One. Tametsi's promise of logic-based solutions made the strategy seem professionally weak. Shawna asked me to explain a move. I pointed confidently. She waited. Tank said confidence was not a number, although I had been submitting it as one for years.

The board invited a stricter pleasure: a conclusion that followed from what was visible. Mercedes liked that the game did not need guesses, but she wanted the word difficult printed somewhere I could not cover with my stamp. Rosa liked the possibility of leaving an unfinished puzzle without losing the work, since an interruption should not become an administrative incident. I considered the drawing tools as a place to keep a real argument instead of a speech about my intuition. There was something satisfying about admitting that a tile should remain untouched until the evidence supported it. The department briefly experienced the unfamiliar sensation of having fewer conclusions than claims.
games.pleasure: Tametsi offers demanding logic puzzles about finding hidden mines among tiles. The developer says solutions do not require guessing, provides on-screen drawing tools for notes, and saves progress even within a level. For someone who enjoys careful deduction, those features can support a substantial problem without requiring an immediate answer.
games.burden: The developer also explicitly describes the game as difficult. Large patterns, written notes and relationships between clues can become mentally busy even when the physical action is modest. Verify the click controls, tile visibility and stopping behavior on the device. The inspected text supports automatic progress saving, but it does not explicitly certify every input as hold-free or every activity as untimed.
games.first: Try an early board and write down one deduction with the available note tools. Decide whether the reasoning itself is enjoyable before treating more difficult boards as an objective.
games.ruling: Admit a conclusion when the clues support it. My pointing finger has been demoted from Evidence Department to General Direction Services.

games.title: Mario Paint
games.case_title: The Stamp Department Has Finally Found Its Medium
scene: I had spent several volumes defending stamps as a serious creative instrument. Mario Paint offered a room where that defense might actually stand up. Tank looked at a row of repeated pictures and said I had found a form of bureaucracy with better colors. I chose to accept this as professional recognition.

Rosa wanted to make a small picture without turning the process into an art examination. Mercedes wanted to see what happened when a ridiculous little image was repeated in a pleasing arrangement. Shawna directed us toward stamps and fills before I disappeared into every icon on the screen. The mouse made the old console feel like a tiny studio. I proposed composing the department's official anthem as well, but Tank said we should first establish whether the picture needed fourteen copies of my favorite symbol. It did not. We removed thirteen and suddenly it looked intentional. This remains one of the few documented occasions when reducing my contribution improved the composition.
games.pleasure: The original SNES Mario Paint is a creative toy for pictures, music and animation, built around the SNES Mouse. Stamping and filling areas offer a narrower first activity than exploring the entire toolbox. Its appeal is making something playful, with nostalgia as an optional bonus rather than a requirement.
games.burden: The original hardware needs the mouse peripheral. Manual instructions distinguish simple selections from held-button dragging used by other tools, so the whole program is not hold-free. Many icons and palette choices can create menu clutter. The separate Gnat Attack activity adds reaction demands and is outside this suggested stamp-and-fill trial. This is creation, not a character-story adventure.
games.first: Choose one stamp and one fill color, then make a small picture. Leave freehand dragging, animation and the reaction minigame aside while checking mouse comfort.
games.ruling: Authorize the gold stamp to pursue an artistic career, provided it accepts criticism and does not fill every available inch with evidence of its own existence.
games.source_note: Nintendo announcement confirms the 1992 original; original Nintendo manual transcription, hosted by a third party, distinguishes stamps/fills from held dragging and the separate Gnat Attack activity. Card scope is original SNES Mouse play, not an automatic claim about modern ports.

games.title: Color a Dinosaur
games.case_title: The Dinosaur Has Requested One Color and No Brand Strategy
scene: I prepared a presentation about restoring the dinosaur's public image. Mercedes asked whether the animal had requested this service. I said it had left several areas uncolored, which I considered an invitation to develop a visual identity. Tank said it looked more like an invitation to choose a color.

The attraction here was deliberately narrow: an old console, a picture and a small set of choices. Rosa could see a place for that if someone actually wanted the nostalgia. Shawna could also see the danger of offering it to a person who had asked for a richer story and calling the mismatch kindness. I put the presentation away. The dinosaur did not become a more grown-up mystery because I gave it a committee. It remained a simple coloring toy, available to enjoy on exactly those terms. Mercedes chose a ridiculous color and laughed. That was a good enough reason for the choice; it did not require me to pretend the picture concealed an epic.
games.pleasure: Color a Dinosaur is an original NES coloring toy with a deliberately small activity loop. Its manual describes selecting pictures and filling regions with colors, including a point-to-point control arrangement. It belongs here as a specific retro curiosity for someone who wants that simple action, not as a substitute for adult narrative.
games.burden: The presentation is aimed at young children and the variety is limited. That may be a taste veto regardless of how few controls are needed. The original manual supports the coloring controls, while full-play timing and modern-device behavior have not been tested here. Mode changes can affect the drawing; check the intended setup rather than assuming an emulator reproduces every behavior conveniently.
games.first: If the retro coloring idea itself appeals, fill a few regions in one picture. Stop the trial once its narrow appeal is clear; completing a picture is optional.
games.ruling: Admit the dinosaur only by personal invitation. No amount of executive branding can turn a coloring toy into the grown-up mystery somebody asked for.
games.source_note: Original manual scan, hosted by a third party, was visually examined in the earlier project research (work/retro-games.json); current reopen yielded no searchable text. Manual-supported point-to-point coloring is a narrow option, not a tested whole-game or emulator guarantee. Wrong Steam coloring-game match excluded.

games.title: The Incredible Machine 3
games.case_title: The Ball Will Ring the Bell After Several Avoidable Expenses
scene: I could see the appeal immediately: a simple task achieved through an arrangement so elaborate that everyone else would wonder why I had not just done the task. Tank said the department had finally found its autobiography. I objected because our office did not contain a balloon-powered component. 'Give you another hour,' he said.

The imagined contraption had a ball, a useful object, and more connecting logic than the result strictly required. Shawna wanted to know whether changing one part would explain the failure. Mercedes liked the comedy of an absurd mechanism that genuinely worked. Rosa asked whether we could celebrate a small successful chain without rebuilding the entire table. I agreed, although the agreement was difficult because a pulley seemed like the kind of thing the table had been missing. We kept the experiment modest. A practical outcome reached by a wonderfully impractical route felt like honest entertainment, provided nobody confused it with my preferred method for organizing everybody else's evening.
games.pleasure: The Incredible Machine 3 is a historical contraption-building puzzle candidate: arrange parts into chains of cause and effect to achieve an objective. Its appeal is seeing an unlikely mechanism succeed after a useful adjustment. This 1995 Windows entry is included for a revisit if an existing copy and workable setup are available.
games.burden: Evidence is weaker here than for the modern store entries. A Sierra historical archive identifies the game, but its descriptive text credits a secondary database; the linked scanned manual was located without usable text verification. Exact mouse actions, timers, compatibility and present availability remain unresolved. Do not mistake this historical candidate for a certified easy-to-run or hold-free recommendation.
games.first: On a working existing setup, inspect one introductory contraption and its controls before changing a single component. Avoid turning software setup into the evening's main activity.
games.ruling: Approve a ridiculous machine when its workings are the pleasure. Deny my attempt to use that principle as the department's purchasing policy.

games.title: SimCity 2000 Special Edition
games.case_title: The Mayor Has Built a Monument Before Asking About Water
scene: I laid out a magnificent avenue leading directly to the mayor's office. Tank asked where the residents lived. I said that was the next phase of civic excellence. Shawna asked about utilities. I pointed to the avenue again, which did not improve its ability to supply water.

A city-building game could make these decisions interesting because the city would have reasons to care about them. Mercedes liked the thought of shaping a place, then seeing how its parts related. Rosa preferred a neighborhood people might enjoy to a skyline designed entirely for my portrait. I began to understand why a city was more than a large arrangement of attractive blocks. It also meant that this was not the same kind of evening as placing a few decorative houses. The council could not honestly promise simplicity while handing over a budget. I reduced the proposed monument to a bench, and even that remained conditional on somebody actually having a place to live.
games.pleasure: SimCity 2000 Special Edition offers the classic city-building and management fantasy, with the ability to design a settlement and respond to its needs. The current exact-edition store description includes additional cities and scenarios. It may appeal through nostalgia, long-term planning and the satisfaction of a place taking shape.
games.burden: Management brings budgets, services, tools and simulation behavior into the same interface. This is a meaningful increase in menu and system complexity, not a default low-demand choice. Check speed controls, pausing, the ability to inspect while paused and the readability of the old interface on the intended setup. The reviewed sources do not establish a special no-pressure mode or hold-free operation.
games.first: Inspect an existing city or an introductory situation and identify one service before building extensively. Decide whether managing relationships between systems sounds enjoyable, rather than merely liking the skyline.
games.ruling: Authorize the mayor only if planning is the attraction. The monument budget stays frozen until the ordinary neighborhood has something useful beneath its impressive view.
games.source_note: Exact Special Edition GOG listing and official EA title page inspected. Supports city design/management and edition identity; pause behavior, no-pressure modes and present-device control comfort were not verified.

games.title: RollerCoaster Tycoon Deluxe
games.case_title: The Queue Has Become Longer Than the Official Speech
scene: I designed a grand entrance and prepared to welcome the first guests with a speech. Tank examined the imaginary queue and suggested that people had come for rides. I said the speech would establish the park's values. Mercedes asked whether one of those values was eventually letting people reach a roller coaster.

The park offered both a visual pleasure and an operational problem. Paths, rides and guests could become a place worth looking at, but the visitors also brought needs and expectations. Shawna wanted to start with something already built before allowing me to design an attraction with six official opening ceremonies. Rosa proposed one comfortable corner with a sensible route through it. I began to see why a prebuilt ride could be a useful beginning rather than an insult to creativity. The first successful improvement might be small. I cut the speech to one sentence, which made the queue shorter in spirit even before anybody touched the paths.
games.pleasure: RollerCoaster Tycoon Deluxe combines the original park-management game with its two expansion packs. It offers both custom coaster construction and prebuilt rides, alongside the business of keeping guests and finances in order. The pleasure can be a recognizable little park evolving through practical and creative decisions.
games.burden: Designing rides is only part of the game: management menus, guest needs, money and scenario demands can create pressure. Check simulation speed and pause behavior, exact mouse operations and interface size. The presence of prebuilt rides does not remove the rest of the management system, and this edition should not be credited with modes from later RollerCoaster Tycoon releases.
games.first: Inspect an opening park or scenario and locate one prebuilt attraction in the interface. Evaluate whether the management surrounding construction feels interesting before committing to a large custom coaster.
games.ruling: Approve a park for someone who enjoys designing a place and managing its consequences. My welcoming speech must remain shorter than the path to the first ride.

games.title: Theme Hospital
games.case_title: The Administrator Has Bought a Fountain Instead of a Sensible Floor Plan
scene: I proposed improving institutional confidence with a spectacular entrance. Shawna asked whether the building's actual rooms were ready. I said the fountain would communicate readiness. Tank said it would communicate water, and only if we had remembered the pipe.

Theme Hospital's absurd institution seemed likely to understand the gap between official ambition and everyday operations. Mercedes was interested in the satire but declined any attempt to turn the evening into a real discussion of medical experiences. Rosa agreed: the joke could stay on ridiculous management, especially mine. We imagined the consequences of making a decorative decision while the useful work waited. It was an uncomfortable mirror, although a funny one. I moved the fountain down the plan. Shawna moved it off the plan. Tank suggested replacing it with a sign reading THE ADMINISTRATOR HAS BEEN ASKED TO CONSIDER OTHER PEOPLE. I objected to the length, then recognized that reducing the message would probably make it about me again.
games.pleasure: Bullfrog's original Theme Hospital is a comic management game about designing and running an institution with limited resources. The official EA page emphasizes building, maintaining and managing the hospital while balancing cash and its exaggerated fictional problems. Its appeal is institutional satire and operational tinkering, rather than a rich personal adventure.
games.burden: Staff, rooms, resources and developing demands can make this a busy management choice. Its comic visual style does not remove time pressure or menu work. Check pausing, speed behavior, readable text and the exact mouse controls before assuming a relaxed setup is possible. The humor includes exaggerated illnesses and death, which may simply be the wrong subject for an enjoyable evening.
games.first: Inspect the early building and management interface without committing to an elaborate plan. Decide whether its subject and overlapping responsibilities are appealing before taking on the continuing simulation.
games.ruling: Admit the satire only when its subject is welcome. Reject the fountain until the administrator can explain what useful problem it is supposed to solve.
games.source_note: Official EA page identifies Bullfrog's original 1997 Theme Hospital and building/management with limited resources. The automatic Steam hit was unrelated DLC and is excluded. Exact pause/hold behavior remains to be checked.

games.title: Zoombinis
games.case_title: The Travellers Have Asked Me to Stop Improving Their Names
scene: A group of small blue travellers needed a way forward. I offered a full naming convention, complete with reference numbers and an organizational chart. Rosa said they already had enough to deal with. Tank suggested that helping them through the actual puzzle would be a more convincing welcome.

The old logic-journey idea had an honest attraction: notice a pattern, make a choice, see whether the group could continue. Mercedes wanted the childhood-adventure presentation described plainly so nostalgia could do its own work. Shawna pointed out that an inviting cartoon could still contain a serious rule to figure out. I agreed to stop confusing appearance with difficulty in either direction. Some evenings might welcome these peculiar travellers; others might want a human mystery with complicated motives. Neither preference required a hearing. I retired the naming chart and concentrated on the route. The travellers retained their own identities, and the department was spared an unnecessary argument over whether a person could be filed under Blue.
games.pleasure: This is the 2015 remake of Logical Journey of the Zoombinis, a cartoon adventure built around pattern and logic puzzles. The developer describes twelve puzzle types with several difficulty levels as the travellers seek a new home. It may appeal through nostalgic character, rule discovery and a sequence of distinct reasoning tasks.
games.burden: The child-oriented presentation is a real taste consideration, especially when the desired experience is a grown-up character story. Logic difficulty can increase independently of that appearance. Check the specific puzzle's clicking, dragging, penalties and timing; the store description does not establish a universally untimed or hold-free route. This entry refers to the remake, not every older edition or platform version.
games.first: Try one early puzzle and explain the pattern you think matters. Check whether helping these characters feels charming before investing in harder levels or the larger journey.
games.ruling: Approve the travellers if their particular charm is wanted. The department has no authority to replace personal taste with nostalgia or a compulsory naming system.
